title: Seat a 100 mm wafer on a mask aligner's chuck: flat on two pins, rim on the third, then slide it in
instruction: The wafer has been set down on the mask aligner's chuck. Seat it against the pre-alignment pins: push it only by its edge until its flat rests against the two close pins at the front and its rim against the pin on the left, without pushing it up onto a pin and without touching its top face more than 3 mm in from the rim. Then press the vacuum key, push the transport slide in by its handle to its end stop, and move both hands clear.
context: Contact mask aligners (SUSS MA6, MA8, MJB4) print chip patterns in university nanofabs and packaging fabs. Every exposure starts by hand: 'Place the flat of the wafer against the two pins at the bottom and move the wafer against the last pin on the left' (UCSB MA6 SOP); 'Be sure not to load on top of the pins!' (EPFL MJB4 manual). Then the vacuum goes on and the slide is pushed in. Here the wafer lies loose on the chuck, slightly off and turned, and is pushed by its rim alone, with a closed fingertip, until it sits on three raised pins: an off-centre push turns it flat onto both close pins, then it slides along them to the third. This differs from carrying a wafer with tweezers and orienting it by its flat on a mounter: nothing is carried here; the rim is pushed by fingertips against two flat pins and an edge pin, then the chuck is slid in. The SOPs have the wafer moved against the pins by its rim, which a closed fingertip does here.
setup: Station: two YAM arms with parallel grippers, bases 61 cm apart at the near edge of a 120 x 90 cm table. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Aligner base: a fixed block 30 x 25 x 5 cm centred at (50, 0). The transport slide, a 16 x 14 x 1 cm aluminium plate (top 6.0 cm up, 1 kg with its chuck), rides on two rails along x and is pulled out toward the robot, spanning x 22 to 38; it runs 15 cm in (+x) to an end stop with 3 N of sliding friction. A 8 x 1.2 x 1.2 cm handle bar stands at its near edge at x 21. On it a 120 mm round aluminium vacuum chuck, 10 mm thick, centred at (30, 0), face 7.0 cm up. Three 2 mm steel pins stand 0.4 mm proud of its face (screw-set on real chucks; UCSB MA-6 SOP Rev D): the two close pins' centres at (-48.3, -10) and (-48.3, +10) mm from the chuck's centre, so their faces lie on x = -47.3 where a seated wafer's flat lies; the left pin's centre at (0, +51.0), its face at +50.0. Vacuum key: a push key on the base at (40, +10), 4 mm travel, 3 N. Wafer: silicon, 100.0 mm, 0.525 mm thick, primary flat 32.5 mm (SEMI M1), 9.6 g, lying loose on the chuck (friction 0.3), flat toward the robot, its centre 4 mm farther from the robot and 3 mm to the right of seated and turned 8 degrees clockwise seen from above: its flat is 2.5 mm or more from the close pins and its rim 3 mm from the left pin, so it starts on no pin. Real trial at low cost, no aligner needed: a 300 mm ball-bearing drawer-slide pair with an end stop under a 160 x 140 x 10 mm aluminium plate, a printed handle, on plywood; the chuck is a 120 mm 6061 aluminium disc, 10 mm thick, with three 2 mm ISO 2338 h8 dowel pins in reamed holes set 0.4 mm proud with a feeler gauge (drawing: standin/chuck.svg), a 1 mm ring groove and a 3 mm hole to a hose barb on a small diaphragm pump, switched by a push switch. Wafers: test-grade (dummy) 100 mm silicon wafers, SEMI M1, 525 um, one primary flat. Plate, chuck and handle are machined or printed to the sizes above (no catalogue part needed; any 100 mm, 525 um test-grade wafers). A printed gauge sets the start pose.
scoring: Read at the end with a 0.3 mm feeler gauge at each pin, a photo from above and one from the side, and a ruler on the slide; everything that must hold 'at any time' is read from one continuous video from above. Vacuum on is read from the pump's gauge (or the wafer resisting a light tap). Score 0, and it stays 0 (video), if at any time a fingertip touches the wafer's top face more than 3 mm in from its rim, the wafer rides up onto a pin (tilted over 1 degree or lifted), leaves the chuck or is flicked faster than 0.1 m/s, the wafer cracks or chips, or the slide moves more than 5 mm before the vacuum is on. Otherwise at the end: 0.25 if the flat touches one close pin (photo from above; the feeler does not pass); 0.5 if it touches both close pins, lying flat on the chuck; 0.75 if its rim also touches the left pin and the vacuum is on (the key counts only once the wafer is seated, and must be released); 1.0 if then the slide, pushed by a fingertip at its handle, is at its end stop (within 1 mm), the feeler still does not pass at any pin with the slide in, every fingertip is 5 cm from the wafer and the handle (video), and all is still for 1 s (video).
fidelity: PhysX at 240 Hz. The wafer is a rigid disc whose collider is 1.5 mm box strips. The vacuum is a 30 N downward force on the wafer once the key is pressed; no air flow. Pins are 2 mm cylinders 0.4 mm proud. The slide's 3 N friction and the key's 3 N are settings. The face-touch check reads the centre of a hand's finger ends against the wafer's outline. The aligner's body, mask and optics are not modelled.
scores: Dream-1: 0 (one valid run, 90 s: no seating); demo: 1.0
reset_notes: Nothing is random (object_jitter=0). Between real trials lift the wafer off, vent the chuck, pull the slide out and place the wafer with the printed gauge.
